events_chronological: Child psychologist Aubrey Lang and his wife Frida celebrate a civic award for his work with children.
A former patient named Emory breaks into their bathroom, accuses Aubrey of having failed him, shoots him in the stomach and then kills himself.
Aubrey bleeds to death on the bedroom floor with Frida beside him.
The following autumn Aubrey takes on nine-year-old Toby Salter, a withdrawn boy whose case reminds him of Emory's.
Toby's mother Dana keeps finding cupboards standing open, drawers pulled out and marks on her son's body that she cannot explain.
Toby is shut in a cupboard at a birthday party and comes out hysterical and bruised.
Aubrey arrives late for his wedding anniversary dinner and Frida leaves the restaurant without speaking to him.
Toby finally tells Aubrey that he sees dead people walking around who do not know that they are dead.
Aubrey almost drops the case, then replays the old tape of Emory and hears a terrified voice in another language behind his own.
Aubrey tells Toby to stop running from the ghosts and to listen to what they want from him.
Bree Marlow, a girl who has just died, appears in Toby's tent and hands him a videotape.
At Bree's wake Toby gives her father the tape, which shows her stepmother poisoning her food.
Toby tells his mother about the ghosts and repeats what his dead grandmother heard her say at the graveside, and Dana believes him.
No longer terrified, Toby is cast in the school play and is happy in it.
Aubrey tells Toby that he has helped him and that the two of them will not need to see each other again.
Aubrey goes home, watches his and Frida's wedding video, and sees that she is asleep and has been talking to no one.
Frida's hand opens and Aubrey's wedding ring falls out, and he finds the bullet wound in his own back.
Aubrey tells his sleeping wife that he loves her and lets go.
nonlinear_category_reason: Almost strictly forward, with one suppressed earlier scene - the shooting - withheld until the closing minutes.
syuzhet_notes: The film runs almost strictly forward, and its single displacement is the one that matters: told-order bullet 17 is a flashback to the night of the shooting, suppressed for the whole runtime and released only in the closing montage, which also replays earlier scenes to show that nobody but the boy has spoken to the psychologist since. The nonlinearity here is one withheld event rather than a shuffled timeline.
fabula_notes: The psychologist's death is elided by a caption naming the following season, so the months between the shooting and the new case are inferred rather than shown. That every scene between the psychologist and his wife is a man talking to a woman who cannot hear him is established retroactively and never played as such at the time.

events.content: A framed citation, a glass of wine on the stairs, a wife reading the inscription out loud. He is being told, formally, that he is good at his work.
